body.en: HL Topic 1 extends secondary algebra into foundational university pure mathematics: mathematical induction, proof by contradiction, complex analysis in Cartesian, polar, and exponential representations, de Moivre's theorem, roots of unity, partial fraction decomposition, and algebraic systems.

label.en: ● Level 1 Foundation — Complex Numbers & Argand Plane Geometry

body.en:
A complex number is an ordered pair of real numbers \((a, b)\) written as \(z = a + bi\), where \(i\) is the imaginary unit satisfying \(i^2 = -1\):

\[ \text{Re}(z) = a \in \mathbb{R}, \quad \text{Im}(z) = b \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Fundamental Algebraic Operations:

  • Addition & Subtraction: \((a+bi) \pm (c+di) = (a\pm c) + (b\pm d)i\) — isomorphic to vector addition in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  • Multiplication: \((a+bi)(c+di) = (ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i\).
  • Complex Conjugate: \(\bar{z} = a - bi\). Key properties: \(z\bar{z} = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2\), \(\overline{z_1 z_2} = \bar{z}_1 \bar{z}_2\), and \(\text{Re}(z) = \frac{z+\bar{z}}{2}\), \(\text{Im}(z) = \frac{z-\bar{z}}{2i}\).
  • Division: Realise the denominator by multiplying by the conjugate: \[ \frac{a+bi}{c+di} = \frac{(a+bi)(c-di)}{c^2+d^2} = \frac{ac+bd}{c^2+d^2} + \frac{bc-ad}{c^2+d^2}i. \]
  • Modulus & Principal Argument: The modulus is the Euclidean distance from the origin \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). The principal argument \(\text{Arg}(z) = \theta\) is uniquely defined in the half-open interval \(-\pi < \theta \le \pi\): \[ \theta = \begin{cases} \arctan(b/a) & a > 0 \\ \arctan(b/a) + \pi & a < 0, b \ge 0 \\ \arctan(b/a) - \pi & a < 0, b < 0 \\ \frac{\pi}{2} & a = 0, b > 0 \\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & a = 0, b < 0 \end{cases} \]

label.en: ▲ Level 2 Analytical Tools — De Moivre's Theorem, Roots of Unity & Systems

body.en:
Polar & Euler Representation: Every non-zero complex number can be expressed as: \[ z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta) = r\operatorname{cis}\theta = r e^{i\theta} \] Multiplication scales moduli and adds arguments: \(z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}\). Division divides moduli and subtracts arguments: \(z_1 / z_2 = (r_1/r_2)e^{i(\theta_1 - \theta_2)}\).

De Moivre's Theorem: For any \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\): \[ [r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta) = r^n e^{i n\theta} \]

Multiple-Angle & Power Expansion Identities:

  • To express \(\cos(n\theta)\) or \(\sin(n\theta)\) in powers of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\): expand \((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n\) using the Binomial Theorem and equate real and imaginary parts to \(\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)\).
  • To express \(\cos^n\theta\) or \(\sin^n\theta\) as a sum of multiple angles: substitute \(z = e^{i\theta}\), noting \(z + z^{-1} = 2\cos\theta\) and \(z - z^{-1} = 2i\sin\theta\), then expand \((2\cos\theta)^n = (z + z^{-1})^n\) and group conjugate pairs \(z^k + z^{-k} = 2\cos(k\theta)\).

\(n\)-th Roots of Complex Numbers & Roots of Unity: The \(n\) solutions to \(z^n = w = R e^{i\phi}\) form the vertices of a regular \(n\)-gon centered at the origin on a circle of radius \(R^{1/n}\): \[ z_k = R^{1/n} \exp\left(i\frac{\phi + 2\pi k}{n}\right), \quad k = 0, 1, \dots, n-1. \] In particular, the \(n\)-th roots of unity (solutions to \(z^n = 1\)) are \(\omega^k\) where \(\omega = e^{i 2\pi / n}\). They satisfy the vanishing sum theorem: \[ 1 + \omega + \omega^2 + \dots + \omega^{n-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \omega^k = \frac{\omega^n - 1}{\omega - 1} = 0 \quad (\text{for } n \ge 2). \]

caption.en: The \(n\)-th roots of unity: angle and coordinates of each

ariaLabel.en: Modulus r of z, from 0.5 to 1.5

note.en: \(z = r\)·cis \(\theta\) (indigo) and \(z^{n} = r^{n}\)·cis\((n\theta)\) (amber, dashed) — this is de Moivre's theorem in full: raising \(z\) to the nth power multiplies the angle \(by n\) AND raises the modulus to the nth power. The gray rings are the \(n\)-th roots of unity (always on the unit circle, \(r = 1\)), \(k = 0\), …, \(n - 1\), evenly spaced \(360^\circ / n\) apart starting at angle \(0^\circ\). Set \(r = 1\) and drag \(\theta\) to a multiple of that spacing to land \(z^{n}\) exactly on \(z = 1\), the \(k = 0\) root. Push \(r\) above or below 1 and watch \(z^{n}\) leave the unit circle — outward for \(r\) > 1, inward for \(r\) < 1 — since \(|z^{n}| = r^{n}\) grows or shrinks with \(n\), unlike the roots of unity themselves.

body.en:
Partial Fraction Decomposition: Let \(p(x)/q(x)\) be a proper rational function (\(\deg p < \deg q\)). Factor \(q(x)\) over \(\mathbb{R}\):

  • Distinct linear factors: \(\frac{p(x)}{(x-a)(x-b)} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{x-b}\).
  • Repeated linear factors: \(\frac{p(x)}{(x-a)^2(x-b)} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{(x-a)^2} + \frac{C}{x-b}\).
  • Irreducible quadratic factors \(x^2+bx+c\) (with \(b^2-4c < 0\)): \[ \frac{p(x)}{(x-a)(x^2+bx+c)} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}. \]

Geometric Classification of 3×3 Systems: A system of 3 linear equations in 3 unknowns represents 3 planes \(\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\):

  • Unique Solution (Rank 3): \(\det(A) \neq 0\). The 3 planes intersect at a single point.
  • Infinitely Many Solutions (Rank 2, Consistent): Elimination yields \(0 = 0\). Geometrically, the planes either intersect along a common line (pencil of planes) or two/three planes are coincident.
  • No Solution (Inconsistent): Elimination yields \(0 = k\) with \(k \neq 0\). Geometrically, the planes form a triangular prism (sheaf with parallel lines of intersection) or two or more planes are parallel and distinct.

label.en: ▲ Level 3 University Rigor — Theorem: Proof Theory & Algebra Fundamentals

body.en:
Principle of Mathematical Induction: Let \(P(n)\) be a predicate for \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\). If (1) \(P(1)\) is true (Base Step), and (2) for every \(k \ge 1\), \(P(k) \implies P(k+1)\) (Inductive Step), then \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).
Proof via Well-Ordering Principle: Suppose the set \(S = \{n \in \mathbb{Z}^+ : eg P(n)\}\) is non-empty. By the Well-Ordering Principle of \(\mathbb{Z}^+\), \(S\) contains a least element \(m\). Since \(P(1)\) is true, \(m > 1\), so \(m-1 \ge 1\). Because \(m-1 < m\), \(m-1 otin S\), which means \(P(m-1)\) is true. But by the Inductive Step, \(P(m-1) \implies P(m)\), contradicting that \(m \in S\). Thus \(S = \emptyset\). \( lacksquare\)

Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum): To prove proposition \(P\), assume \( eg P\) is true and derive a logical contradiction \(Q \land eg Q\).
Theorem: \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.
Proof: Assume for contradiction that \(\sqrt{2} = rac{p}{q}\) with \(p, q \in \mathbb{Z}^+\) and \(\gcd(p, q) = 1\). Squaring gives \(2 = rac{p^2}{q^2} \implies p^2 = 2q^2\). Thus \(p^2\) is even, which implies \(p\) is even (since the square of an odd integer is odd: \((2m+1)^2 = 4m^2+4m+1\)). Let \(p = 2k\). Then \((2k)^2 = 2q^2 \implies 4k^2 = 2q^2 \implies q^2 = 2k^2\). Thus \(q^2\) is even, so \(q\) is even. But then \(2 \mid p\) and \(2 \mid q\), contradicting \(\gcd(p, q) = 1\). Therefore \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational. \( lacksquare\)

Conjugate Root Theorem: If \(P(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k\) is a polynomial with real coefficients (\(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\)) and \(P(z_0) = 0\), then \(P(\overline{z_0}) = 0\).
Proof: Using properties of complex conjugation (\(\overline{u+v} = ar{u}+ ar{v}\), \(\overline{uv} = ar{u} ar{v}\), and \( ar{a}_k = a_k\) for \(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\)): \[ P(\overline{z_0}) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k (\overline{z_0})^k = \sum_{k=0}^n \overline{a_k z_0^k} = \overline{\sum_{k=0}^n a_k z_0^k} = \overline{P(z_0)} = ar{0} = 0. \quad lacksquare \] Consequently, non-real complex roots of real polynomials always occur in conjugate pairs \(a \pm bi\), and their product gives an irreducible real quadratic factor \((z - z_0)(z - \overline{z_0}) = z^2 - 2 ext{Re}(z_0)z + |z_0|^2\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Algebra, Proof & Complex Numbers)

body.en:
Why De Moivre's Theorem & Conjugate Root Pairing Hold: By Euler's identity \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), raising \(z = re^{i\theta}\) to the \(n\)-th power gives:

\[ z^n = \left(re^{i\theta}\right)^n = r^n e^{in\theta} = r^n(\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)) \]

Furthermore, if \(P(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k\) has real coefficients (\(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\)), taking complex conjugates across \(P(z_0) = 0\) uses \(\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar{z}_1 + \bar{z}_2\) and \(\bar{a}_k = a_k\) to prove \(P(\bar{z}_0) = \overline{P(z_0)} = 0\). Thus non-real roots of real polynomials always occur in conjugate pairs \(\alpha \pm i\beta\).

label.en: Worked Example 1.1 — Inductive Proof of Divisibility

problem.en: Prove by mathematical induction that \(5^n + 2\cdot 3^{n-1} + 1\) is divisible by 8 for all positive integers \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

solution.en:
Base Step (\(n = 1\)):
For \(n = 1\): \[ 5^1 + 2\cdot 3^0 + 1 = 5 + 2(1) + 1 = 8. \] Since \(8 = 8(1)\), the proposition is true for \(n = 1\).

Inductive Hypothesis:
Assume the proposition is true for \(n = k \ge 1\), meaning: \[ 5^k + 2\cdot 3^{k-1} + 1 = 8M \quad \text{for some integer } M \in \mathbb{Z}. \] Hence \(5^k = 8M - 2\cdot 3^{k-1} - 1\).

Inductive Step (\(n = k + 1\)):
Evaluate the expression for \(n = k + 1\): \[ 5^{k+1} + 2\cdot 3^k + 1 = 5\cdot 5^k + 2\cdot 3^k + 1. \] Substitute the inductive hypothesis for \(5^k\): \[ = 5\left(8M - 2\cdot 3^{k-1} - 1\right) + 2\cdot 3^k + 1 \] \[ = 40M - 10\cdot 3^{k-1} - 5 + 2\cdot 3\cdot 3^{k-1} + 1 \] \[ = 40M - 10\cdot 3^{k-1} + 6\cdot 3^{k-1} - 4 \] \[ = 40M - 4\cdot 3^{k-1} - 4 = 40M - 4(3^{k-1} + 1). \] Notice that \(3^{k-1}\) is always odd for any integer \(k \ge 1\), so \(3^{k-1} + 1\) is always an even integer, say \(2p\) for \(p \in \mathbb{Z}\). Therefore: \[ = 40M - 4(2p) = 40M - 8p = 8(5M - p). \] Since \(M, p \in \mathbb{Z}\), \(5M - p\) is an integer. Thus the expression is divisible by 8.

Conclusion:
Since the base case \(n=1\) holds, and if true for \(n=k\) then true for \(n=k+1\), by the principle of mathematical induction the statement is true for all \(n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\).

label.en: Worked Example 1.2 — Multiple Angle Trig Derivation via De Moivre

problem.en: Use De Moivre's Theorem to express \(\cos 4\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\). Hence solve the equation \(8x^4 - 8x^2 + 1 = 0\).

solution.en:
1. By De Moivre's Theorem: \[ \cos 4\theta + i\sin 4\theta = (\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^4. \] 2. Expand using the Binomial Theorem with \(c = \cos\theta, s = \sin\theta\): \[ = c^4 + 4c^3(is) + 6c^2(is)^2 + 4c(is)^3 + (is)^4 = c^4 + 4ic^3s - 6c^2s^2 - 4ics^3 + s^4. \] 3. Equate real parts: \[ \cos 4\theta = c^4 - 6c^2s^2 + s^4. \] Substitute \(s^2 = 1 - c^2\): \[ \cos 4\theta = c^4 - 6c^2(1 - c^2) + (1 - c^2)^2 = c^4 - 6c^2 + 6c^4 + 1 - 2c^2 + c^4 = 8c^4 - 8c^2 + 1. \] Thus \(\cos 4\theta = 8\cos^4\theta - 8\cos^2\theta + 1\).

4. To solve \(8x^4 - 8x^2 + 1 = 0\), set \(x = \cos\theta\): \[ \cos 4\theta = 0 \implies 4\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} + k\pi \implies \theta = \frac{\pi}{8} + \frac{k\pi}{4} \quad (k = 0, 1, 2, 3). \] Evaluating for \(k = 0, 1, 2, 3\) yields four distinct real roots: \[ x = \cos\frac{\pi}{8}, \quad \cos\frac{3\pi}{8}, \quad \cos\frac{5\pi}{8} = -\cos\frac{3\pi}{8}, \quad \cos\frac{7\pi}{8} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{8}. \]

label.en: Worked Example 1.3 — Partial Fractions with Irreducible Quadratic

solution.en:
1. Formulate the decomposition: \[ \frac{3x^2 + 5x + 8}{(x - 1)(x^2 + 4)} = \frac{A}{x - 1} + \frac{Bx + C}{x^2 + 4}. \] 2. Clear denominators: \[ 3x^2 + 5x + 8 = A(x^2 + 4) + (Bx + C)(x - 1). \] 3. Evaluate at \(x = 1\) (Heaviside cover-up for \(A\)): \[ 3(1)^2 + 5(1) + 8 = A(1 + 4) + 0 \implies 16 = 5A \implies A = \frac{16}{5}. \] 4. Expand and compare coefficients: \[ 3x^2 + 5x + 8 = (A + B)x^2 + (C - B)x + (4A - C). \] Comparing \(x^2\) terms: \[ A + B = 3 \implies B = 3 - \frac{16}{5} = -\frac{1}{5}. \] Comparing constant terms: \[ 4A - C = 8 \implies C = 4\left(\frac{16}{5}\right) - 8 = \frac{64 - 40}{5} = \frac{24}{5}. \] 5. Verify \(x\) coefficient: \(C - B = \frac{24}{5} - \left(-\frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{25}{5} = 5\) (Checks out!).

Final Decomposition: \[ \frac{16}{5(x-1)} + \frac{-x + 24}{5(x^2+4)}. \]

label.en: Worked Example 1.4 — Solving a 3×3 System by Elimination

solution.en:
Label the equations (1), (2), (3). Add (1) and (3) to eliminate \(z\): \((x+y+z)+(x+2y-z)=6+2\Rightarrow2x+3y=8\) — call this (4).

Subtract (2) from (1) to eliminate \(z\) again: \((x+y+z)-(2x-y+z)=6-3\Rightarrow-x+2y=3\Rightarrow x=2y-3\) — call this (5).

Substitute (5) into (4): \(2(2y-3)+3y=8\Rightarrow4y-6+3y=8\Rightarrow7y=14\Rightarrow y=2.\)

Then \(x=2(2)-3=1\), and from (1): \(1+2+z=6\Rightarrow z=3.\)

Check in (2): \(2(1)-2+3=3.\) ✓ Check in (3): \(1+2(2)-3=2.\) ✓

Solution: \((x,y,z)=(1,2,3)\) — the unique point where all three planes meet.

label.en: ⚠ Topic 1 Exam Traps: Proof by Induction & Complex Roots

body.en:
Induction Conclusion Statement: IB mark schemes reserve an explicit final mark (R1) for the full concluding sentence: 'Since true for n=1, and if true for n=k then true for n=k+1, by mathematical induction the statement is true for all n ∈ ℤ⁺.' Omitting this loses the mark.

Principal Argument Interval: In IB AA HL, the argument must satisfy \(-\pi < \operatorname{Arg}(z) \le \pi\). Angles like \(300^\circ\) or \(\dfrac{5\pi}{3}\) must be rewritten as \(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

Partial Fraction Degree Check: For improper rational fractions where degree of numerator \(\ge\) degree of denominator, you must perform polynomial division before setting up partial fractions.

rows.en: Places a 2nd-quadrant complex number in the 4th quadrant.
Forgets \(i^2 = -1\), flipping the sign of \(bd\) in the real part.
Group real and imaginary parts carefully: \((ac - bd) + (ad + bc)i\).
Fails to rewrite in standard form \(|z - z_0| = r\).
Factor out the minus sign: \(|z - (-4 + 6i)| = 4 \implies z_0 = (-4, 6)\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Algebra, Proof & Complex Numbers

body.en: Exam Verification Tip (IB Diploma Mathematics: AA / AI Higher Level (Papers 1, 2 & 3)): Always check complex division \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\) by verifying that \(|z_1 / z_2| = |z_1| / |z_2|\). If the moduli ratio does not match, you multiplied the denominator by \(a + bi\) instead of the conjugate \(a - bi\).

question.en: Solve the equation \(z^3 + 8 = 0\), expressing all solutions in Cartesian form \(a + bi\).

solution.en:
Write \(z^3 = -8 = 8e^{i\pi}\). By De Moivre's Theorem, the three cube roots are: \[ z_k = 2\exp\left(i\frac{\pi + 2\pi k}{3}\right) \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, 2. \] For \(k = 0\): \(z_0 = 2e^{i\pi/3} = 2\left(\frac{1}{2} + i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 1 + i\sqrt{3}\).
For \(k = 1\): \(z_1 = 2e^{i\pi} = 2(-1) = -2\).
For \(k = 2\): \(z_2 = 2e^{i 5\pi/3} = 2e^{-i\pi/3} = 2\left(\frac{1}{2} - i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 1 - i\sqrt{3}\).
Notice that \(1 \pm i\sqrt{3}\) are complex conjugates, as predicted by the Conjugate Root Theorem for \(z^3 + 8 \in \mathbb{R}[z]\).

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(z^3 = -8 = 8e^{i\pi}\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: [Practice 2 · Hard] Let \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) be complex numbers such that \(z_1 = 2 + i\) and \(z_2 = 3 - 2i\). \newline Consider the complex number \(w = \frac{z_1^2}{z_2}\). \newline If \(w = a + bi\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are real numbers, find the value of \(a^2 + b^2\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the mathematical relationship in Algebra, Proof & Complex Numbers and write down the given values.
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Substitute the known quantities into the governing equation or formula and simplify step by step.
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Verify that your final result satisfies all conditions stated in the problem.

solution.en: First, we calculate \(z_1^2\): \( z_1^2 = (2 + i)^2 = 4 + 4i + i^2 = 4 + 4i - 1 = 3 + 4i \). ewline Next, we calculate \(w = rac{z_1^2}{z_2} = rac{3 + 4i}{3 - 2i}\). ewline To simplify, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: \( w = rac{(3 + 4i)(3 + 2i)}{(3 - 2i)(3 + 2i)} = rac{9 + 6i + 12i + 8i^2}{9 - 4i^2} = rac{9 + 18i - 8}{9 + 4} = rac{1 + 18i}{13} = rac{1}{13} + rac{18}{13}i \). ewline So, \(a = rac{1}{13}\) and \(b = rac{18}{13}\). ewline We need to find \(a^2 + b^2\): \( a^2 + b^2 = \left( rac{1}{13} ight)^2 + \left( rac{18}{13} ight)^2 = rac{1}{169} + rac{324}{169} = rac{325}{169} \). ewline Simplifying the fraction: \( rac{325}{169} = rac{25 imes 13}{13 imes 13} = rac{25}{13} \). ewline Alternatively, we can use the property that \(|w| = rac{|z_1|^2}{|z_2|}\). Then \(|w|^2 = \left( rac{|z_1|^2}{|z_2|} ight)^2 = rac{|z_1|^4}{|z_2|^2}\). ewline \(|z_1|^2 = 2^2 + 1^2 = 4 + 1 = 5\). \(|z_2|^2 = 3^2 + (-2)^2 = 9 + 4 = 13\). \(a^2 + b^2 = |w|^2 = rac{5^2}{13} = rac{25}{13}\). [M1] [A1]
